claim: T. carassii infection of 5 dpf zebrafish larvae leads to approximately 10-20% survival by 15 days post infection (dpi).
source: Similar to the previous report, T. carassii infection of 5 dpf zebrafish larvae leads to approximately 10–20% survival by 15 days post infection (dpi) with the highest incidence of mortality between 4 and 7dpi (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by survival curve data shown in Figure 1A and described in the text.

claim: The highest incidence of mortality during T. carassii infection occurs between 4 and 7 days post infection.
source: Similar to the previous report, T. carassii infection of 5 dpf zebrafish larvae leads to approximately 10–20% survival by 15 days post infection (dpi) with the highest incidence of mortality between 4 and 7dpi (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by survival curve data shown in Figure 1A indicating mortality timing.

claim: The onset of mortality coincided with the peak of parasitaemia as assessed by real-time quantitative gene expression analysis of a T. carassii-specific gene.
source: The onset of mortality coincided with the peak of parasitaemia as assessed by real-time quantitative gene expression analysis of a T. carassii-specific gene (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 1B correlating with mortality timing.

claim: 10-20% of zebrafish larvae survive T. carassii infection, suggesting that zebrafish larvae can control T. carassii infection.
source: Nevertheless, we consistently observed 10–20% survival in the T. carassii-infected group, suggesting that zebrafish larvae can control T. carassii infection.
evidence: Based on inference from survival data showing a subset of larvae survive.

claim: From 4 dpi onwards, larvae can be consistently sorted into groups of high- or low-infected individuals based on in vivo observations without sacrificing animals.
source: From 4 dpi onwards, we could consistently sort larvae into groups of high- or low-infected individuals based on in vivo observations, without the need to sacrifice animals (Video 1).
evidence: Supported by the clinical scoring system described and demonstrated in Video 1.

claim: Infection levels were categorised using four criteria: escape reflex, infection scores based on parasite:blood cell ratio, extravasation, and vasodilation.
source: Infection levels were categorised using four criteria: (1) escape reflex (slow vs fast) upon contact with a pipette tip, (2) infection scores (1–10, see details in Materials and methods), based on the ratio of blood cells and parasites passing through an intersegmental capillary (ISC) in 100 events (Figure 2A,B) (Video 1, 00:06-00:39 s), (3) extravasation, based on the presence of parasites outside of blood vessels (Figure 2C) (Video 1, 00:40-1:20 s) and (4) vasodilation, based on the diameter of the caudal vein (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: Described in text and illustrated in Figure 2 and Video 1.

claim: Individuals with an infection score between 2 and 3 (~80%) were categorised as low-infected and had a high survival rate (relative percent survival, 82%).
source: Individuals with an infection score between 2 and 3 (~80%, Figure 2F) were categorised as low-infected and had a high survival rate (relative percent survival, 82%; Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2F and 2G.

claim: Individuals with an infection score between 6 and 10 (~20%) were categorised as high-infected and generally succumbed to the infection.
source: Individuals with an infection score between 6 and 10 (~20%, Figure 2F) were categorised as high-infected and generally succumbed to the infection (Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2F and 2G.

claim: In individuals categorised as high-infected, T. carassii-specific gene expression increased more than 60-fold.
source: As expected, in individuals categorised as high-infected, T. carassii-specific gene expression increased more than 60-fold, whereas in low-infected individuals the increase was less than 20-fold (Figure 2H).
evidence: Supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: In low-infected individuals, T. carassii-specific gene expression increased less than 20-fold.
source: As expected, in individuals categorised as high-infected, T. carassii-specific gene expression increased more than 60-fold, whereas in low-infected individuals the increase was less than 20-fold (Figure 2H).
evidence: Supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Total neutrophil response (total green fluorescence) was not significantly affected by T. carassii infection.
source: Total neutrophil response (total green fluorescence) was not significantly affected by the infection (Figure 3A and C).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence quantification data shown in Figure 3A and 3C.

claim: The macrophage response (total red fluorescence) increased significantly in infected individuals from 3 dpi onwards.
source: In contrast, the macrophage response (total red fluorescence) increased significantly in infected individuals from 3 dpi onwards, and was most prominent in the head region and along the posterior cardinal vein and caudal vein (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence quantification data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: In low-infected larvae, a significant increase in red fluorescence was observed already by 5 dpi and remained high up until 9 dpi.
source: In low-infected larvae, a significant increase in red fluorescence was observed already by 5 dpi and remained high up until 9 dpi; in high-infected larvae, despite a marginal but not significant increase at 5 and 7 dpi, significant differences to the PVP group were observed at day nine after infection (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence quantification data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In high-infected larvae, significant differences in red fluorescence to the PVP group were observed at day nine after infection.
source: In low-infected larvae, a significant increase in red fluorescence was observed already by 5 dpi and remained high up until 9 dpi; in high-infected larvae, despite a marginal but not significant increase at 5 and 7 dpi, significant differences to the PVP group were observed at day nine after infection (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence quantification data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: No significant differences in macrophage fluorescence were observed between high- or low-infected individuals.
source: Interestingly, no significant differences were observed between high- or low-infected individuals, suggesting that despite the clear differences in trypanosome levels (Figure 2H), overall macrophages number appeared to be influenced more by the presence than by the total number of trypanosomes.
evidence: Based on statistical analysis of fluorescence data in Figure 3C.

claim: Overall macrophage number appeared to be influenced more by the presence than by the total number of trypanosomes.
source: Interestingly, no significant differences were observed between high- or low-infected individuals, suggesting that despite the clear differences in trypanosome levels (Figure 2H), overall macrophages number appeared to be influenced more by the presence than by the total number of trypanosomes.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that macrophage numbers are similar despite different parasite loads.

claim: EdU+ macrophages were observed in all groups, and their number was higher in low- and high-infected individuals compared to PVP-injected controls.
source: There, EdU+ macrophages could be observed in all groups, and in agreement with the total cell fluorescence measured in the same region (Figure 4C), their number was higher in low- and high-infected individuals compared to PVP-injected controls (Figure 4D and corresponding Video 2).
evidence: Supported by EdU+ cell counting data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: No significant difference in EdU+ macrophage number was observed between high- and low-infected fish.
source: No significant difference was observed between high- and low-infected fish, confirming that the macrophage number is affected by the presence and not by the number of trypanosomes.
evidence: Based on statistical analysis of EdU+ macrophage counts.

claim: T. carassii infection triggers macrophage division and this is higher in infected compared to non-infected individuals.
source: Altogether, these data confirm that T. carassii infection triggers macrophage division and that this is higher in infected compared to non-infected individuals, possibly due to a higher haematopoietic activity.
evidence: Based on EdU incorporation data showing proliferating macrophages.

claim: In high-infected larvae, a large proportion of macrophages were observed around and inside the caudal vein, the majority of which were EdU+.
source: Within the trunk region of high-infected larvae, a large proportion of macrophages were observed around and inside the caudal vein, the majority of which were EdU+ (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that in high-infected larvae, recently divided macrophages migrated to the vessels.
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In infected fish, a significant, although low number of EdU+ neutrophils was present.
source: Interestingly, quantification of EdU+ neutrophils in the trunk region, revealed that while in PVP-injected individuals EdU+ neutrophils were rarely observed, in infected fish, a significant, although low number of EdU+ neutrophils was present (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by EdU+ neutrophil counting data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Neutrophils respond to T. carassii infection by dividing, but their number is relatively low.
source: These data indicate that neutrophils also respond to the infection by dividing, but their number is relatively low and may not significantly contribute to changes in total cell fluorescence.
evidence: Based on EdU+ neutrophil data and total fluorescence measurements.

claim: Neutrophils were never observed within the posterior cardinal vein or caudal vein.
source: In contrast to macrophages, within the analysed trunk region, neutrophils were never observed within the posterior cardinal vein or caudal vein, and independently of whether they were EdU+ or not, were mostly observed lining the vessel (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: T. carassii triggers a differential macrophage and neutrophil response, with a significant increase in macrophages number likely due to enhanced myelopoiesis.
source: Altogether, these data indicate that, independent of the trypanosome number, T. carassii triggers a differential macrophage and neutrophil response, with a significant increase in macrophages number likely due to enhanced myelopoiesis.
evidence: Based on EdU incorporation data and cell distribution analysis.

claim: In PVP controls, both macrophages and neutrophils were exclusively located outside the caudal vein in close contact with the endothelium or in the tissue adjacent the vessel.
source: In PVP controls, both macrophages and neutrophils were exclusively located outside the caudal vein in close contact with the endothelium or in the tissue adjacent the vessel.
evidence: Supported by imaging data in Figure 6A.

claim: In infected fish, neutrophils remained exclusively outside the vessels.
source: In infected fish, while neutrophils remained exclusively outside the vessels (Figure 6A, left panel and 7B), macrophages could be seen both inside (white arrows) and outside (blue arrows) the caudal vein (Figure 6A, right panel and Figure 6C, left plot).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: In infected fish, macrophages could be seen both inside and outside the caudal vein.
source: In infected fish, while neutrophils remained exclusively outside the vessels (Figure 6A, left panel and 7B), macrophages could be seen both inside (white arrows) and outside (blue arrows) the caudal vein (Figure 6A, right panel and Figure 6C, left plot).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: In high-infected larvae, macrophages inside the caudal vein clearly had a more rounded morphology.
source: Whilst in low-infected individuals macrophage morphology was similar to that observed in non-infected fish, in high-infected larvae, macrophages inside the caudal vein clearly had a more rounded morphology (Figure 6A, right panel and Figure 6D, right plot).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6A and quantification in Figure 6D.

claim: Differently from neutrophils, macrophages increase in number in infected fish, are recruited inside the caudal vein and, depending on the infection level, their morphology can be greatly affected.
source: Altogether these data indicate that differently from neutrophils, macrophages increase in number in infected fish, are recruited inside the caudal vein and, depending on the infection level, their morphology can be greatly affected.
evidence: Based on imaging and quantification data from Figures 6 and 7.

claim: In high-infected larvae, large, dark, granular and round macrophages were consistently observed located inside the caudal vein generally on the dorsal luminal side.
source: Strikingly, in high-infected larvae, we consistently observed large, dark, granular and round macrophages located inside the caudal vein generally on the dorsal luminal side.
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The occurrence of large, granular macrophages increased with the progression of the infection and was exclusive to high-infected individuals.
source: The occurrence of these large, granular macrophages increased with the progression of the infection (Video 5) and was exclusive to high-infected individuals as they were never observed in low-infected or control larvae.
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Video 5.

claim: Administration of BODIPY-FL5 in infected larvae revealed the accumulation of lipids in large macrophages.
source: Interestingly, administration of BODIPY-FL5 in infected larvae one day prior to the expected appearance of the large macrophages, revealed the accumulation of lipids in these cells (Video 6).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Video 6 and Figure 7B.

claim: BODIPY+ macrophages occur only in high-infected individuals.
source: Quantification of the number of BODIPY+ and BODIPY- macrophages, confirmed that BODIPY+ macrophages occur only in high-infected individuals (Figure 7C).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The large, rounded, granular macrophages in the caudal vein are foamy macrophages.
source: These results therefore confirms that the large, rounded, granular macrophages in the caudal vein are indeed foamy macrophages.
evidence: Based on BODIPY staining showing lipid accumulation in these cells.

claim: All large foamy macrophages were strongly positive for tnfa.
source: Our results clearly show that all large foamy macrophages, were strongly positive for tnfa, suggesting an inflammatory activation state (Figure 8A).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: All foamy macrophages within the caudal vein were also positive for il1b.
source: Similar to what observed for tnfa expression, all foamy macrophages within the caudal vein were also positive for il1b (Figure 8C, asterisk), confirming their pro-inflammatory profile.
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Foamy macrophages occur in high-infected larvae and have a strong pro-inflammatory profile.
source: Altogether these data indicate that foamy macrophages occur in high-infected larvae and have a strong pro-inflammatory profile.
evidence: Based on tnfa and il1b expression data in foamy macrophages.

claim: High-infected individuals exhibited a higher pro-inflammatory response than low-infected larvae.
source: When comparing the overall inflammatory state in high- and low-infected larvae it was apparent that high-infected individuals exhibited a higher pro-inflammatory response (Figure 9).
evidence: Supported by imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 9.

claim: A higher number of tnfa- and il1b-expressing cells was observed in high-infected larvae compared to low-infected larvae.
source: Although tnfa- and il1b-positive macrophages could be seen in low-infected individuals, these were generally few (Figure 9A and Figure 9B middle panels, Figure 9C) and a higher number of tnfa- and il1b-expressing cells was observed in high-infected larvae (Figure 9A and Figure 9B right panels, Figure 9C).
evidence: Supported by imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 9.

claim: Not only the number of tnfa:eGFP+ cells but also the intensity of their eGFP signal is higher in high-infected compared to PVP or low-infected individuals.
source: The images confirm that tnfa expression is strongly inducible in leukocytes and that not only the number of tnfa:eGFP+ cells but also the intensity of their eGFP signal is higher in high-infected compared to PVP or low-infected individuals.
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: In high-infected individuals, uncontrolled parasitaemia leads to an exacerbated pro-inflammatory response associated with susceptibility to the infection.
source: Altogether, these results suggest that in high-infected individuals, uncontrolled parasitaemia leads to an exacerbated pro-inflammatory response associated with susceptibility to the infection.
evidence: Based on correlation between high parasitaemia, high inflammatory markers, and mortality.

claim: Low-infected individuals, with moderate il1b and tnfa responses, are able to control parasitaemia and to recover from the infection.
source: Low-infected individuals, however, with moderate il1b and tnfa responses, are able to control parasitaemia and to recover from the infection.
evidence: Based on correlation between low parasitaemia, moderate inflammatory markers, and survival.

claim: Innate immunity is sufficient to control first-peak parasitaemia during trypanosome infection of zebrafish.
source: Altogether these data confirm that also during trypanosome infection of zebrafish, innate immunity is sufficient to control first-peak parasitaemia and that a controlled inflammatory response is beneficial to the host.
evidence: Based on observations in zebrafish larvae lacking adaptive immunity.

claim: A controlled inflammatory response is beneficial to the host during trypanosome infection of zebrafish.
source: Altogether these data confirm that also during trypanosome infection of zebrafish, innate immunity is sufficient to control first-peak parasitaemia and that a controlled inflammatory response is beneficial to the host.
evidence: Based on correlation between moderate inflammation and survival in low-infected individuals.

claim: T. carassii infection triggers macrophage division, particularly in low-infected individuals.
source: Using transgenic lines marking macrophages and neutrophils, total cell fluorescence and cell proliferation analysis revealed that T. carassii infection triggers macrophage division, particularly in low-infected individuals.
evidence: Based on EdU incorporation and fluorescence data.

claim: Phagocytosis can be excluded as a contributing factor to parasitaemia control since motile T. carassii cannot be engulfed by any innate immune cell.
source: Phagocytosis however, can be excluded as one of the possible contributing factors since motile T. carassii, similar to other extracellular trypanosomes (Caljon et al., 2018; Saeij et al., 2003; Scharsack et al., 2003), cannot be engulfed by any innate immune cell (Video 7).
evidence: Supported by video evidence shown in Video 7 and citations.

claim: In low-infected individuals, only moderate il1b or tnfα expression was observed, mostly in macrophages.
source: A strong inflammatory response is also not required for trypanosomes control, since in low-infected individuals, only moderate il1b or tnfα expression was observed, mostly in macrophages, as assessed using transgenic zebrafish reporter lines.
evidence: Based on imaging data from transgenic reporter lines.

claim: Recombinant zebrafish (as well as carp and trout) Tnfα are all able to directly lyse T. brucei.
source: Although we were unable to investigate the specific role of Tnfα during T. carassii infection of zebrafish, due to the unavailability of tnfα-/- zebrafish lines or the unsuitability of morpholinos for transient knock-down at late stages of development, we previously reported that recombinant zebrafish (as well as carp and trout) Tnfα, are all able to directly lyse T. brucei (Forlenza et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Forlenza et al., 2009).

claim: During Trypanoplasma borreli infection of common carp, soluble as well as transmembrane carp Tnfα play a crucial role in both trypanosome control and susceptibility to the infection.
source: In the same study, we reported that also during Trypanoplasma borreli (kinetoplastid) infection of common carp, soluble as well as transmembrane carp Tnfα play a crucial role in both, trypanosome control and susceptibility to the infection.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: The direct lytic activity of zebrafish Tnfα may have played a role in the control of first-peak parasitaemia in low-infected individuals.
source: Thus, considering the evolutionary conservation of the lectin-like activity among vertebrate's TNFα (Daulouède et al., 2001; Forlenza et al., 2009; Lucas et al., 1994; Magez et al., 1997), it is possible that the direct lytic activity of zebrafish Tnfα may have played a role in the control of first-peak parasitaemia in low-infected individuals.
evidence: Based on inference from evolutionary conservation and previous studies.

claim: While TNFα production is required for parasitaemia control, a timely shedding of TNFα Receptor-2 (TNFR2) is necessary to limit TNFα-mediated infection-associated immunopathology.
source: Using various comparative mice infection models, it became apparent that while TNFα production is required for parasitaemia control, a timely shedding of TNFα Receptor-2 (TNFR2) is necessary to limit TNFα-mediated infection-associated immunopathology (Radwanska et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Radwanska et al., 2018.

claim: During T. brucei infection in mice and cattle, continuous cleavage of membrane glycosyl-phosphatidyl-inisotol (GPI)-anchored VSG (mVSG-GPI) leads to shedding of the soluble VSG-GIP (sVSG-GPI).
source: Furthermore, during T. brucei infection in mice and cattle, continuous cleavage of membrane glycosyl-phosphatidyl-inisotol (GPI)-anchored VSG (mVSG-GPI) leads to shedding of the soluble VSG-GIP (sVSG-GPI), while the di-myristoyl-glycerol compound (DMG) is left in the membrane.
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on T. brucei.

claim: The galactose-residues of sVSG-GPI constituted the minimal moiety required for optimal TNFα production.
source: While the galactose-residues of sVSG-GPI constituted the minimal moiety required for optimal TNFα production, the DMG compound of mVSG contributed to macrophage overactivation (TNFα and IL-1β secretion) (Magez et al., 2002; Magez et al., 1998; Sileghem et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to Magez et al., 2002; Magez et al., 1998; Sileghem et al., 2001.

claim: T. carassii possesses a surface dominated by GPI-anchored carbohydrate-rich mucin-like glycoproteins, not subject to antigenic variation.
source: Although T. carassii was shown to possess a surface dominated by GPI-anchored carbohydrate-rich mucin-like glycoproteins, not subject to antigenic variation (Lischke et al., 2000; Overath et al., 2001), components of its excreted/secreted proteome, together with phospholipase C-cleaved GPI-anchored surface proteins, have all been shown to play a role in immunogenicity (Joerink et al., 2007), inflammation (Oladiran and Belosevic, 2010; Oladiran and Belosevic, 2009; Ribeiro et al., 2010) as well as immunosuppression (Oladiran and Belosevic, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies on T. carassii.

claim: Neutrophils were never observed inside the cardinal caudal vein although in infected individuals they were recruited and observed in close contact with the outer vessel's endothelium.
source: Neutrophils were never observed inside the cardinal caudal vein although in infected individuals they were certainly recruited and were observed in close contact with the outer vessel's endothelium.
evidence: Based on imaging data from transgenic lines marking vasculature and neutrophils.

claim: In low-infected individuals the majority of macrophages recruited to the cardinal caudal vein remained outside the vessel in close contact with the endothelium.
source: While in low-infected individuals the majority of macrophages recruited to the cardinal caudal vein remained outside the vessel in close contact with the endothelium, in high-infected individuals the majority of macrophages were recruited inside the caudal vein and were tightly attached to the luminal vessel wall.
evidence: Based on imaging data from transgenic lines marking vasculature and macrophages.

claim: In high-infected individuals the majority of macrophages were recruited inside the caudal vein and were tightly attached to the luminal vessel wall.
source: While in low-infected individuals the majority of macrophages recruited to the cardinal caudal vein remained outside the vessel in close contact with the endothelium, in high-infected individuals the majority of macrophages were recruited inside the caudal vein and were tightly attached to the luminal vessel wall.
evidence: Based on imaging data from transgenic lines marking vasculature and macrophages.

claim: Foam cells, or foamy macrophages have been named after the lipid bodies accumulated in their cytoplasm leading to their typical enlarged morphological appearance.
source: Foam cells, or foamy macrophages have been named after the lipid bodies accumulated in their cytoplasm leading to their typical enlarged morphological appearance (Dvorak et al., 1983), but are also distinguished by the presence of diverse cytoplasmic organelles (Melo et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dvorak et al., 1983 and Melo et al., 2003.

claim: Foam cells have been shown to be typical of atherosclerotic plaques associated to various inflammatory metabolic diseases as well as cancer and autoimmune diseases.
source: Foam cells have been shown to be typical of atherosclerotic plaques associated to various inflammatory metabolic diseases (e.g. hyperlipidemia, diabetes, insulin resistance and obesity) as well as cancer (e.g. Papillary renal cell carcinoma, Esophageal xanthoma and non-small cell lung carcinoma) and autoimmune diseases e.g. multiple sclerosis, systemic lupus erythematosus, rheumatoid arthritis (reviewed in Guerrini and Gennaro, 2019; Saka and Valdivia, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Foamy macrophages have been associated with several (intracellular) infectious diseases, including Leishmaniasis, Chagas disease, experimental malaria, toxoplasmosis, tuberculosis and other intracellular bacterial infections.
source: Besides inflammatory diseases, they have also been associated with several (intracellular) infectious diseases, including Leishmaniasis, Chagas disease, experimental malaria, toxoplasmosis, tuberculosis and other intracellular bacterial infections (reviewed in Guerrini and Gennaro, 2019; López-Muñoz et al., 2018; Vallochi et al., 2018) but never before with (extracellular) trypanosome infection.
evidence: Supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Foamy macrophages have never before been associated with (extracellular) trypanosome infection.
source: Besides inflammatory diseases, they have also been associated with several (intracellular) infectious diseases, including Leishmaniasis, Chagas disease, experimental malaria, toxoplasmosis, tuberculosis and other intracellular bacterial infections (reviewed in Guerrini and Gennaro, 2019; López-Muñoz et al., 2018; Vallochi et al., 2018) but never before with (extracellular) trypanosome infection.
evidence: Based on review of literature and current findings.

claim: During T. cruzi infection of rat, increased numbers of activated monocytes or macrophages were reported in the blood or heart.
source: For example, during T. cruzi infection of rat, increased numbers of activated monocytes or macrophages were reported in the blood or heart (Melo and Machado, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Melo and Machado, 2001.

claim: Trypanosome uptake was shown to directly initiate the formation of lipid bodies in macrophages, leading to the appearance of foamy macrophages.
source: Interestingly, trypanosome uptake was shown to directly initiate the formation of lipid bodies in macrophages, leading to the appearance of foamy macrophages (D'Avila et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to D'Avila et al., 2011.

claim: During human Mycobacterium tuberculosis infections, foamy macrophages play a role in sustaining the presence of bacteria and contribute to tissue cavitation enabling the spread of the infection.
source: During human Mycobacterium tuberculosis infections, foamy macrophages play a role in sustaining the presence of bacteria and contribute to tissue cavitation enabling the spread of the infection (Russell et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Russell et al., 2009.

claim: Foamy macrophages are generally associated with inflammation, since their cytoplasmic lipid bodies are a source of eicosanoids, strong mediators of inflammation.
source: Independently of the disease, it is clear that foamy macrophages are generally associated with inflammation, since their cytoplasmic lipid bodies are a source of eicosanoids, strong mediators of inflammation (Melo et al., 2006; Wymann and Schneiter, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Melo et al., 2006 and Wymann and Schneiter, 2008.

claim: Inflammatory mediators such as Prostaglandin E2 benefit trypanosome survival, as shown in Trypanosoma, Leishmania, Plasmodium, and Toxoplasma infections.
source: In turn, inflammatory mediators such as Prostaglandin E2 benefit trypanosome survival, as shown in Trypanosoma, Leishmania, Plasmodium, and Toxoplasma infections (reviewed in Vallochi et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to review article Vallochi et al., 2018.

claim: The occurrence of foamy macrophages was observed exclusively in individuals that developed high parasitaemia, characterised by a strong pro-inflammatory response, and ultimately succumbed to the infection.
source: Our results are consistent with these reports as we show the occurrence of foamy macrophages exclusively in individuals that developed high parasitaemia, characterised by a strong pro-inflammatory response, and ultimately succumbed to the infection.
evidence: Based on correlation between foamy macrophages, high parasitaemia, inflammation, and mortality.

claim: The increase in trypanosome number preceded the appearance of foamy macrophages.
source: Although we did not systematically investigate the exact kinetics of parasitaemia development in correlation with foamy macrophages occurrence, during our in vivo monitoring, we consistently observed that the increase in trypanosome number preceded the appearance of foamy macrophages.
evidence: Based on in vivo observations during monitoring.

claim: In high-infected individuals, foamy macrophages may be formed due to the necessity to clear the increasing concentration of circulating trypanosome-derived moieties or of dying trypanosomes.
source: It is possible that, in high-infected individuals, foamy macrophages are formed due to the necessity to clear the increasing concentration of circulating trypanosome-derived moieties or of dying trypanosomes.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on observations.

claim: The occurrence of foamy macrophages has been reported for intracellular trypanosomatids (T. cruzi, Leishmania).
source: The occurrence of foamy macrophages has been reported for intracellular trypanosomatids (T. cruzi, Leishmania), and arachidonic acid-derived lipids were reported to act as regulators of the host immune response and trypanosome burden during T. brucei infections (López-Muñoz et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to López-Muñoz et al., 2018.

claim: This study is the first to report the presence of foamy macrophages during an extracellular trypanosome infection.
source: To our knowledge, our study is the first to report the presence of foamy macrophages during an extracellular trypanosome infection.
evidence: Based on review of literature and current findings.

claim: The zebrafish model paves the way to investigate which mediators of the trypanosomes are responsible for the induction of inflammatory response and study the conditions that lead to the formation of foamy macrophages in vivo.
source: Our model paves the way to investigate which mediators of the trypanosomes are responsible for the induction of such inflammatory response as well as study the conditions that lead to the formation of foamy macrophages in vivo.
evidence: Based on the establishment of the zebrafish-T. carassii infection model.

claim: Trypanosomes of the Trypanosoma genus are protozoan haemoflagellates that can infect animals from all vertebrate classes.
source: Trypanosomes of the Trypanosoma genus are protozoan haemoflagellates that can infect animals from all vertebrate classes, including warm-blooded mammals and birds as well as cold-blooded amphibians, reptiles, and fish.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about Trypanosoma.

claim: Anaemia appears to be a factor common to infections with most if not all trypanosomes although with different underlying causative mechanisms.
source: Pathologically, anaemia appears to be a factor common to infections with most if not all trypanosomes although with different underlying causative mechanisms.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about trypanosome pathology.

claim: Infections with trypanosomes are often associated with dysfunction and pathology related to exacerbated innate and adaptive immune responses.
source: Immunologically, infections with trypanosomes are often associated with dysfunction and pathology related to exacerbated innate and adaptive immune responses (reviewed by Radwanska et al., 2018; Stijlemans et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Innate immune mediators such as IFNγ, TNFα, and nitric oxide (NO) were shown to be indispensable for the control of first-peak parasitaemia.
source: Instead, innate immune mediators such as IFNγ, TNFα, and nitric oxide (NO) were shown to be indispensable for the control of first-peak parasitaemia, through direct and indirect mechanisms (reviewed by Radwanska et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to review article Radwanska et al., 2018.

claim: In the early phase of infection, the timely induction of IFNγ by NK, NKT, and CD8+ cells followed by the production of TNFα and NO by IFNγ-primed macrophages leads to effective control of first-peak parasitaemia.
source: In the early phase of infection, the timely induction of IFNγ by NK, NKT, and CD8+ cells Cnops et al., 2015 followed by the production of TNFα and NO by IFNγ-primed macrophages (Baral et al., 2007; Iraqi et al., 2001; Lopez et al., 2008; Lucas et al., 1994; Magez et al., 1993; Magez et al., 2007; Magez et al., 2006; Magez et al., 2001; Magez et al., 1999; O'Gorman et al., 2006; Sternberg and Mabbott, 1996; Wu et al., 2017) leads to effective control of first-peak parasitaemia.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to studies on trypanosome immunity.

claim: An early innate immune response is crucial to control the acute phase of trypanosome infection, but its tight regulation is critical to ensure parasite control as opposed to pathology.
source: Altogether, these data made clear that an early innate immune response is crucial to control the acute phase of trypanosome infection, but that its tight regulation is critical to ensure parasite control as opposed to pathology.
evidence: Based on synthesis of multiple studies on trypanosome immunity.

claim: Infections with T. carassii present many of the pathological features observed during human or animal trypanosomiasis, including a pro-inflammatory response during first-peak parasitaemia.
source: Previous studies in common carp (Cyprinus carpio), goldfish (Carrassius aurata) and more recently zebrafish, demonstrated that infections with T. carassii present many of the pathological features observed during human or animal trypanosomiasis, including a pro-inflammatory response during first-peak parasitaemia (Kovacevic et al., 2015; Oladiran et al., 2011; Oladiran and Belosevic, 2009) polyclonal B and T cell activation (Joerink et al., 2007; Joerink et al., 2004; Lischke et al., 2000; Ribeiro et al., 2010; Woo and Ardelli, 2014) and anaemia (Dóró et al., 2019; Islam and Woo, 1991; McAllister et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to studies on T. carassii infections.

claim: Shared features among human and animal (including fish) trypanosomiases suggest a commonality in (innate) immune responses to trypanosomes across different vertebrates.
source: These shared features among human and animal (including fish) trypanosomiases suggest a commonality in (innate) immune responses to trypanosomes across different vertebrates.
evidence: Based on inference from comparative pathology across species.

claim: During the first 2-3 weeks of development, zebrafish are devoid of mature T and B lymphocytes and thus offer a window of opportunity to study innate immune responses.
source: During the first 2–3 weeks of development, zebrafish are devoid of mature T and B lymphocytes and thus offer a window of opportunity to study innate immune responses (Torraca et al., 2014; Torraca and Mostowy, 2018), especially those driven by neutrophils and macrophages.
evidence: Supported by citations to Torraca et al., 2014 and Torraca and Mostowy, 2018.

claim: This is the first report of the occurrence of foamy macrophages during an extracellular trypanosome infection.
source: This is the first report of the occurrence of foamy macrophages during an extracellular trypanosome infection.
evidence: Based on review of literature and current findings.
